743.title: How are the mighty fallen (2 Samuel 1:17–27)
743.hook: David's lament for Saul and Jonathan
743.howItsDone: Jews read David's lament in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets; the refrain how are the mighty fallen comes three times in the song, in verses 19, 25 and 27.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the woman of Endor set bread before a king who'd lost all his strength. Your line was she fed him. Did you feed someone who was low? Today, news reaches David from the battle. Day seven hundred forty-three.

Two objects are set down in front of David: a crown, and the band from a king's arm. The young man who brings them has come three days from the battle. Saul has fallen on Mount Gilboa. Jonathan has fallen with him. On paper, this is good news for David. The man who threw spears at him, who chased him through caves and deserts, is gone. The road to the throne is open. And David tears his own clothes. He and his men mourn and weep and fast until evening. Then David does something more. He makes a song.
screen: `SAUL AND JONATHAN, DEAD ON GILBOA.` → `THE ROAD TO THE THRONE IS OPEN.` → `DAVID TEARS HIS CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: The text says David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and over Jonathan, and that it's written in the Book of Jashar. It opens with the beauty of Israel slain on the heights, and then the line it keeps coming back to: "How are the mighty fallen!" It isn't a statement. It's a cry. How. As if the mind can't make it fit. Then David says, don't tell it in Gath, don't announce it in the streets of Ashkelon, the Philistine cities, so their daughters won't rejoice. He curses the hills of Gilboa: no dew, no rain. And then the hardest part. He praises Saul. Saul and Jonathan, lovely and pleasant in their lives, not divided even in death, swifter than eagles, stronger than lions. Daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who dressed you in scarlet and put gold on your clothing. Not a word about the spear. Not a word about the cave. David doesn't pretend Saul was good to him. He just chooses, for the length of a song, to grieve the king and not the enemy. Then the song narrows to one person. I'm distressed for you, my brother Jonathan. Your love to me was wonderful. And the refrain comes back, once more at the very end: how are the mighty fallen, and the weapons of war perished. Some people are easy to grieve. Some aren't. This song holds both kinds at once, the friend and the man who hunted him, and it gives each of them honest tears.
screen: `WRITTEN IN THE BOOK OF JASHAR.` · `TELL IT NOT IN GATH.` · `WEEP OVER SAUL.` · then, large: `HOW ARE THE MIGHTY FALLEN.` · then: `MY BROTHER JONATHAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: grieve a complicated person. Settle, and breathe. Let someone come to mind who is gone, or gone from your life, and who was hard: a parent who hurt you, a boss, an ex, a friend who turned. You don't need to forgive them or excuse anything. Just look for one true thing worth mourning. Something they gave. A way they were strong. Who they might have been. Let it be sad, and let it be mixed. If you pray, you can hold David's cry: how are the mighty fallen. The bell holds the time.
How are the mighty fallen. David's cry over Saul, who hunted him, and Jonathan, who loved him, in one song. Today's word.
screen: `HOW ARE THE MIGHTY FALLEN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: how are the mighty fallen. Today, say one good, true thing about someone who was hard to love. Out loud or on paper. Day seven hundred forty-three.

744.title: With all his might (2 Samuel 6:14–16)
744.hook: the king dances before the ark; Michal despises it
744.howItsDone: Jews read David's dance before the ark in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and dancing with joy in worship carries on in Jewish life, as when people dance with the Torah scrolls on Simchat Torah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, David's lament for Saul and Jonathan. Your line was how are the mighty fallen. Did you find one true thing to grieve in someone hard? Today, the same man, and his whole body full of joy. Day seven hundred forty-four.

Shouting. The blast of the shofar. A crowd pressing up the road into Jerusalem, and in the middle of it, the ark of the covenant, carried up into the city. David is king now. He could ride beside it in robes, nodding to the crowd. Instead, he's out in front of it, in the dust of the road, and he's dancing. Not a polite sway. The kind of dancing that makes people stare. And up above the street, at a window, someone is watching him do it. The same woman who once lowered him through a window to save his life.
screen: `SHOUTING AND THE SHOFAR.` → `THE ARK COMES TO JERUSALEM.` → `A FACE AT THE WINDOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse: "And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod." With all his might. The Hebrew is b'chol oz, with all strength. Nothing held back for his dignity. And notice what he's wearing. Not the king's robes. A linen ephod, a simple garment, the kind the text gives to priests and to the boy Samuel serving at the shrine. Some translators render his dancing as whirling. The next verses add leaping. A king spinning and jumping in the street. Then the camera moves to the window. Michal, the daughter of Saul, looks out, sees King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and the text says she despised him in her heart. Notice how she's named. Not David's wife. The daughter of Saul, as if the old house is looking down at the new one. When David comes home, she meets him with sarcasm: how the king of Israel honored himself today, uncovering himself in front of the servants' maids. And David answers that it was before the Lord that he danced, and he'll be humbler still. Some readers hold this scene up as a picture of joy in God that doesn't stop to ask how it looks. Others make room for Michal's side: the woman at the first window gave everything for David, and at the second window she's only watching. Between those two windows, the book has told us, Saul gave her to another man, and David later had her taken back, while that husband walked behind her, weeping. It shows us a king who forgot himself, and a woman who couldn't.
screen: `B'CHOL OZ: WITH ALL STRENGTH.` · `A LINEN EPHOD, NOT ROBES.` · `MICHAL DESPISES HIM.` · then, large: `WITH ALL HIS MIGHT.` · then: `BEFORE THE LORD I DANCED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: dance without caring who's watching. If you're somewhere private, stand up. If you're not, or you can't stand, you can do this sitting: shoulders, hands, head, feet. Put on a song in your head, or a real one. Something that makes you glad. Then move to it, with all your might, for the length of the bell. Not well. Not for anyone. If a voice in your head says you look ridiculous, keep going anyway. If you pray, you can let the movement be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
With all his might. A king in a linen garment, dancing in the road before the ark, holding nothing back. Today's word.
Your line: with all his might. Today, do one glad thing full out, without checking who's looking. Day seven hundred forty-four.

745.title: At my table (2 Samuel 9)
745.hook: David seeks Jonathan's lame son and seats him at his table always
745.howItsDone: Jews read the story of Mephibosheth in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, as an example of chesed, loyal kindness, kept across generations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, David danced before the ark in a linen ephod. Your line was with all his might. What did you do full out? Today, the king remembers an old promise. Day seven hundred forty-five.

A question, asked in a palace: is there anyone still left of the house of Saul, so I can show him kindness for Jonathan's sake? David is settled now. He has a city and an army. A new king asking after the old king's family could sound like a threat. But David is remembering a field, and arrows, and an oath Jonathan made him swear: the Lord between me and you, between my children and your children. Someone remembers a name. A servant of Saul's house called Ziba. They send for him.
screen: `IS ANYONE LEFT OF SAUL'S HOUSE?` → `FOR JONATHAN'S SAKE.` → `SEND FOR ZIBA.`

segments.voice: Ziba says yes. There's a son of Jonathan, lame in his feet, living in a place called Lo-debar, in someone else's house. His name is Mephibosheth. Earlier the book tells how it happened: he was a small child when the news came from the battle where his father and grandfather died, and his nurse snatched him up and ran, and he fell. He has lived ever since as the leftover of a fallen house. David sends for him. Mephibosheth comes in and falls on his face. He has every reason to be afraid. David says his name, Mephibosheth, and he answers, here is your servant. Then David tells him, fear not. Then the promise. I will surely show you kindness for Jonathan your father's sake. I will give you back all the land of Saul. And you will eat bread at my table continually. The Hebrew word for kindness here is chesed, loyal love, the faithfulness you owe because of a bond. When David first asked Ziba, he even called it the kindness of God. Mephibosheth can hardly take it in. He calls himself a dead dog. David doesn't argue with him. He just keeps the promise. Ziba and his household are told to work the land for Mephibosheth, and David says he'll eat at the king's table like one of the king's sons. The chapter ends with two facts side by side. Mephibosheth ate always at the king's table. And he was lame in both his feet. Nothing about him had to change to get a seat. The table changed. David kept faith with a friend who was gone by keeping a place for his son.
screen: `A SON OF JONATHAN, LAME IN HIS FEET.` · `FEAR NOT.` · `CHESED: LOYAL LOVE.` · then, large: `ALWAYS AT MY TABLE.` · then: `LIKE ONE OF THE KING'S SONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep faith with a friend's family. Settle, and breathe. Let one friend come to mind who has died, or moved far away, or whom you've simply lost touch with. Now think of the people they left behind: a partner, a child, a parent, a sibling. Someone who might be living, in a small way, in Lo-debar. Ask yourself what a seat at your table would look like for them. A dinner. A message on the anniversary. A story about their person they haven't heard. Choose one. If you pray, you can hold their names. The bell holds the time.
At my table. David's chesed to Jonathan's son: land given back, and a seat at the king's table, always. Today's word.
Your line: always at my table. Today, reach out to someone who belongs to a friend you've lost, and make them a place. Day seven hundred forty-five.

746.title: Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11)
746.hook: the king sees, takes, and arranges a loyal husband's death
746.howItsDone: Jews read the story of David and Bathsheba in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and the next chapter, the prophet Nathan's rebuke, is read as part of the same story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonathan's son sat down at David's table, lame in both feet, a place kept for him always. Your line was always at my table. Did you make a place for someone? Today, the same king, in a chapter that turns against him. Day seven hundred forty-six.

At the turn of the year, the text says, the time when kings go out to battle. So David sends his general Joab, and his servants, and the whole army. And David stays in Jerusalem. That one detail sits at the start of the chapter like a stone in a shoe. The king isn't where kings go. One evening he gets up from his bed and walks on the roof of the king's house. And from the roof he sees a woman washing herself, and she is very beautiful. He doesn't look away. He sends someone to find out who she is.
screen: `WHEN KINGS GO OUT TO BATTLE.` → `DAVID STAYS IN JERUSALEM.` → `A WOMAN SEEN FROM THE ROOF.`

segments.voice: The answer comes back with names: Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam, wife of Uriah the Hittite. Married. Her husband is away, fighting in David's own army. Listen to the verbs that follow, all of them the king's. He sees. He sends. He takes. The text gives Bathsheba almost no words in this chapter. The few she sends are a message: I am with child. Then David starts covering. He calls Uriah home from the front and tells him, go down to your house. Uriah doesn't. He sleeps at the palace door with the servants. When David asks why, Uriah says the ark and Israel and Judah are living in tents, and my lord Joab is camped in the open field. How could I go home, eat and drink, and lie with my wife? David gets him drunk. He still won't go home. So David writes a letter to Joab and sends it with Uriah himself. Put Uriah in the front of the hardest fighting, then pull back from him, so he's struck down. Uriah carries his own death in his hand. It happens. Word comes back. And David sends a reply to Joab that sounds almost calm: don't let this thing be evil in your eyes. The sword devours one as well as another. Bathsheba mourns her husband. Then David brings her into his house. And the narrator, who has said nothing about right and wrong all chapter, speaks once: "But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD." In Hebrew it's an echo. David said, let it not be evil in your eyes. The narrator says, it was evil in the eyes of the Lord. The king could see a woman on a roof. He couldn't see what he was doing.
screen: `HE SEES. HE SENDS. HE TAKES.` · `URIAH WON'T GO HOME.` · `THE LETTER IN URIAH'S HAND.` · then, large: `IT DISPLEASED THE LORD.` · then: `HE COULDN'T SEE HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one way power blinds. Power turns up in ordinary places. Over a child, a younger sibling, an employee, a waiter, a partner who needs you, someone who owes you. Settle, and breathe. Let one of those places come to mind. Then ask, quietly: where might my power stop me from seeing this person clearly? What do I get to not notice, because I don't have to? Don't punish yourself. Just find one thing, and name it to yourself in a few words. If you pray, you can hold it before God. The bell holds the time.
Bathsheba. The woman the king saw, sent for and took, while her loyal husband slept at the palace door. Today's word.
Your line: power can blind. Today, look once more at the person you named, and do one thing that treats them as fully seen. Day seven hundred forty-six.

747.title: Thou art the man (2 Samuel 12:1–7)
747.hook: Nathan's parable of the poor man's ewe lamb ends "Thou art the man"
747.howItsDone: Jews read Nathan's parable as part of the book of Samuel, among the Former Prophets, and some teachers use it as a model of how to rebuke someone with care, so that they can actually hear it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bathsheba: a king on a rooftop who saw, took, and then arranged for a loyal soldier to die. Your line was power can blind. Did you name one way it blinds? Today, someone comes to open the king's eyes. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

A prophet walks into the palace with a case for the king to judge. That's all it looks like. Nathan doesn't mention a rooftop, or a soldier, or a letter carried to the front. He tells a story about two men in one city. One is rich, with flocks and herds. The other has nothing at all except one little ewe lamb. The king leans in to listen, the way a judge listens. He has no idea the story is about him. By the time he finds out, he has already passed sentence.
screen: `A PROPHET BRINGS A CASE.` → `TWO MEN IN ONE CITY.` → `THE KING LEANS IN.`

segments.voice: Listen to how Nathan builds the lamb. The poor man bought her and raised her. She grew up with him and with his children. She ate from his own bread, drank from his own cup, slept in his arms. The text says she was to him like a daughter. Every detail makes her harder to lose. Then a traveler comes to the rich man. He doesn't want to take from his own flock, so he takes the poor man's lamb and serves her for dinner. David's anger burns. As the Lord lives, he says, the man who did this deserves to die. He shall pay back the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing and had no pity. And Nathan answers, short and plain: "Thou art the man." Why a story? A king who can arrange a death at the front is not an easy man to accuse. A direct charge might have been brushed aside, or worse. So Nathan goes around the defenses. He lets David's own sense of justice wake up first, about someone else, where it's easy. Then he turns it around. The judge has written his own verdict. Notice what the story leaves out, too. In the parable, the lamb is taken and eaten. In what David actually did, there was a woman, and a husband who was killed. The parable can't carry all of it, and Nathan doesn't pretend it can. Right after the story, he speaks plainly, in God's name: you had everything, and if that were too little, more would have been given. Why did you despise the word of the Lord? A story opened the door. Plain speech walks through it. And one more thing. David is still the king, with every power to silence the man in front of him. In this story, the prophet's job is to tell a king a truth he doesn't want to hear, and everything now turns on whether the king will listen.
screen: `THE LAMB WAS LIKE A DAUGHTER.` · `DAVID PASSES SENTENCE.` · then, large: `THOU ART THE MAN.` · then: `A STORY OPENS THE DOOR.` · `THEN PLAIN SPEECH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to let someone tell you a hard truth. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who sees you clearly: a friend, a sibling, a partner, a coworker who doesn't flatter. Now think of something they might say to you that you'd rather not hear. You don't need to agree with it yet. Just let it sit in the room without arguing back. Notice where in your body the defenses rise. Breathe into that spot. Then decide whether you'll ask them, this week, what they really think. If you pray, you can ask for ears that can hear. The bell holds the time.
Thou art the man. The line that turns a story into a mirror, spoken by a prophet to a king. Today's word.
Your line: thou art the man. Today, when you catch yourself judging someone else's story, ask whether it's also yours. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

748.title: I have sinned (2 Samuel 12:13)
748.hook: David answers in two Hebrew words, with no excuse
748.howItsDone: Jews speak of teshuvah, returning, as naming a wrong, regretting it, and changing course; David's answer to Nathan can be read alongside Psalm 51, which its heading links to this moment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nathan's story of the ewe lamb, and the line that turned it into a mirror. Your line was thou art the man. Did you let anyone tell you something hard? Today, the king answers. Day seven hundred forty-eight.

Nathan has just finished speaking. The room is quiet. A king who has had a man killed now stands accused, in his own palace, by someone with no army behind him. There are plenty of things a king could say next. He could call the guards. He could explain the pressures of war. He could point out that Uriah died in battle, which, on paper, is true. He could ask who else knows. The text gives him none of those lines. It gives him one short answer.
screen: `THE ROOM GOES QUIET.` → `A KING COULD SAY MANY THINGS.` → `HE SAYS ONE.`

segments.voice: Here it is: "I have sinned against the LORD." In Hebrew it's two words, chatati l'Adonai. No because. No but. No list of reasons. It helps to hear it next to another king. Back in the first book of Samuel, Saul is confronted by the prophet Samuel after he disobeys a command. Saul also says I have sinned. And then he keeps going: because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice. The confession comes with a reason attached, and the reason does some of the work of an excuse. David's sentence stops where it starts. Nathan's reply comes just as fast: the Lord has put away your sin; you shall not die. That doesn't mean nothing follows. The very next words say the child born to David will die, and the chapters ahead are full of trouble in his house. Forgiveness here is real, and so are the consequences. The text holds both and doesn't flatten either. Jewish tradition has a name for this kind of turning: teshuvah, returning. And the heading of Psalm fifty-one ties that psalm to this very moment, when Nathan the prophet came to David. Some readers hear that psalm as the long version of what David said here in two words. So what makes this short answer matter? Not that David feels bad. A person can feel bad and still explain. It's that he stops defending himself. He names what he did, and who it was against, and lets it stand. Some readers notice the oddness of the target: he wronged Uriah, and Bathsheba, and the people he commanded. Yet he says, against the Lord. Some hear that as the deepest admission, that every wrong to a person is also a wrong before God. The sentence is short. It is not small.
screen: `TWO WORDS IN HEBREW. NO BECAUSE.` · `SAUL SAID IT, THEN EXPLAINED.` · then, large: `I HAVE SINNED AGAINST THE LORD.` · then: `FORGIVEN, AND STILL CONSEQUENCES.` · `PSALM 51 LOOKS BACK HERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: admit one wrong without an excuse. Settle, and breathe. Let one recent thing come to mind where you got it wrong: a sharp word, a broken promise, a corner cut. Now say it to yourself in one plain sentence. I did this. Then notice the urge to add because, and let the because go. You don't need to explain it right now. Just let the sentence stand on its own. If there's someone you owe that sentence to, picture saying it to them, short, with nothing after it. If you pray, you can bring it before God the same way. The bell holds the time.
I have sinned. David's answer to Nathan, chatati in Hebrew: a confession with no excuse attached. Today's word.
Your line: I have sinned. Today, when you apologize for anything, even something small, stop before the because. Day seven hundred forty-eight.

749.title: The child dies (2 Samuel 12:15–23)
749.hook: David fasts while the child lives, then rises and eats: "I shall go to him"
749.howItsDone: In Jewish mourning, people grieve fully and then, step by step, return to ordinary life; David's rising and eating after the child's death is sometimes taught alongside those customs, though the customs come from later law.

segments.voice: Yesterday, David's answer to Nathan, with no because. Your line was I have sinned. Did you stop before the excuse? Today, the consequence Nathan named arrives, and David does something no one around him expects. Day seven hundred forty-nine.

The servants are whispering in the hallway, and that is how the king finds out. Night after night he has lain on the ground. He hasn't eaten. The elders of his house stood over him and tried to lift him up, and he wouldn't get up and wouldn't eat with them. Now the child is gone, and nobody wants to be the one to say it. If he was like this while the boy lived, they ask each other, what will he do when he hears? David sees them whispering. He asks: is the child dead? And they say: he is dead.
screen: `ON THE GROUND ALL NIGHT.` → `THE SERVANTS WHISPER.` → `IS THE CHILD DEAD?`

segments.voice: This part of the chapter opens with a hard sentence: the Lord struck the child, and he was very sick. Readers have wrestled with that line, and it's fair to let it stay hard. The child did nothing. The text doesn't explain it away, and neither will we. What it does tell, in detail, is what David did. While the boy was alive, David pleaded with God for him, fasted, and lay on the earth. On the seventh day the child died. And then the surprise. David gets up from the ground. He washes, anoints himself, changes his clothes. He goes into the house of the Lord and bows down. Then he comes home, asks for food, and eats. His servants can't make sense of it. You wept while he lived, and now you rise and eat? His answer is plain. While the child was alive, I fasted and wept, because I thought: who knows? Maybe God will be gracious, and the child will live. But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? "I shall go to him," he says, but he will not return to me. Readers hear that last line in more than one way. Some hear only the grave: every person will one day go where the child has gone. Some hear a quiet hope of meeting again. The text doesn't decide for us. What it shows clearly is a turn. As long as something could still change, David fought for it with everything he had. When it could no longer change, he stopped fighting it, washed his face, and went on living. That isn't the same as not caring. The man who rises and eats is the same man who lay on the ground all night.
screen: `THE CHILD IS STRUCK. IT STAYS HARD.` · `FASTING WHILE HE LIVES.` · `HE RISES, WASHES, EATS.` · then, large: `I SHALL GO TO HIM.` · then: `FIGHT WHILE IT CAN CHANGE. THEN RISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept one thing that can't be changed. Settle, and breathe. Let something come to mind that you keep pushing against: a loss, a decision that's already made, a door that has closed. Ask honestly, is there anything left I can do? If there is, name it, and save it for later. If there isn't, let your hands open on your lap, palms up. Breathe out slowly. You're not saying it doesn't matter. You're letting it be what it is. If you pray, you can place it before God. The bell holds the time.
The child dies. David fasts and pleads while the boy lives, then rises, washes and eats when he's gone. Today's word.

Your line: I shall go to him. Today, if something can't be changed, wash your face and take one ordinary step. And look back at this week: how are the mighty fallen, with all his might, always at my table, power can blind, thou art the man, I have sinned, and I shall go to him. Day seven hundred forty-nine.
